title: Clickjacking - Alice's Cupcakes (SEED Labs TP)
description: Hands-on system-security lab on clickjacking (UI redress attack): build a malicious page with an iframe and an invisible button, defend with a frame-busting script, bypass it with the iframe sandbox attribute, and finally block the attack with X-Frame-Options and Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors. Flags are unique for every student (variant sandboxes). Scored out of 20 (platform shows x10 = 200 points).
prerequisites: Basic knowledge of HTML, CSS and JavaScript
Basic Linux command line and Docker usage
Basic knowledge of the HTTP protocol (requests, responses, headers)
outcomes: Explain how a clickjacking attack works and why it is dangerous
Build a clickjacking attack with an iframe and a transparent overlay button
Implement and bypass a JavaScript frame-busting defense (iframe sandbox)
Configure X-Frame-Options and Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors on an Apache server

levels.title: Welcome and grading rules
levels.content:
# Clickjacking TP - *Alice's Cupcakes*

**Read this page carefully, it explains how you are graded.**

## Story
*Alice's Cupcakes* is a small local bakery with a nice website. Alice has heard about clickjacking (a "UI redress attack") and asks you to find out whether her site can be abused. You will play both roles:

1. The attacker - build a malicious page that loads Alice's site in an iframe and hides an invisible button over her real *Explore Menu* button (Tasks 1-2).
2. The defender - protect the site with a frame-busting script (Task 3), watch the attacker bypass it with the sandbox attribute (Task 4), then fix the problem properly on the server side with HTTP headers (Task 5).

## Your environment
You get your own sandbox: one SEED Ubuntu VM (`seed`). The two websites run in Docker containers on that VM (SEED Labs *Clickjacking* lab, folder `~/Labsetup`). Nobody else can see or break your sandbox.

## How the flags work (no copy-paste between classmates)
* Every level has its own flag, generated randomly for your sandbox. A flag from a classmate is simply wrong for you.
* You do not guess a flag: you earn it. When you think a task is done, run in a terminal of the VM

```
sudo cjlab-verify <task number>        # e.g.  sudo cjlab-verify 3
```

  The tool checks your files / the running websites, tells you what is still missing (`[FAIL]` lines) and, once everything is [ OK ], prints your personal flag. Copy it exactly into the answer box.
* You have 10 attempts per level.

## Grading: 20 / 20
The platform works with whole points, so the score is displayed x10: 200 points = 20/20.

| Level | Points shown by the platform | Counts for |
|---|---|---|
| Task 0 - Start the environment | 10 | 1 / 20 |
| Task 1 - Copy that site | 20 | 2 / 20 |
| Task 2 - Let's get clickjacking | 30 | 3 / 20 |
| Task 3 - Bust that frame | 30 | 3 / 20 |
| Task 4 - Bust the buster | 30 | 3 / 20 |
| Task 5 - The ultimate bust | 40 | 4 / 20 |
| Final quiz | 40 | 4 / 20 |
| Total | 200 | 20 / 20 |

**Hints cost points:** each hint removes between 5 and 20 platform points = 0.5 to 2 points out of 20 (the price is written on the hint button). Displaying the full solution gives 0 for that level.

## Rules
* This game is for educational purposes only. Use these techniques only inside your sandbox (10.9.0.x lab containers). Attacking real websites is illegal.
* Besides this game you must hand in the lab report requested by your teacher: screenshots + answers to the questions Q1-Q12 (they are listed in each level) + the important code snippets with explanations.
* The platform records your actions. Work alone.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Your first task is to access the sandbox, where you will complete all following tasks. After you have successfully connected, submit the answer `start`.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview on the right, right-click on `seed` and then click on `Open GUI`; a new pop-up window will appear.
2. Login with username `seed` and password `dees`.

Alternatively, you can use SSH to connect to the machine (handy for copy-paste), but the browsers you need for this lab are in the graphical session. See the documentation for details.

levels.title: Task 0 - Start the lab environment
levels.content:
# Task 0 - Start the lab environment

Two websites are needed in this lab, each one in a Docker container of your VM:

| Role | Container IP | URL |
|---|---|---|
| Defender (Alice's Cupcakes) | 10.9.0.5 | http://www.cjlab.com |
| Attacker (malicious site) | 10.9.0.105 | http://www.cjlab-attacker.com |

The host names are already mapped in /etc/hosts for you.

## To do
1. Open a terminal and go to the lab folder: `cd ~/Labsetup`.
2. Build the images and start the containers (`docker-compose` - see the aliases `dcbuild`, `dcup`).
3. Check with `dockps` that the two containers run.
4. In Firefox open http://www.cjlab.com (Alice's Cupcakes - zoom with Ctrl + / Ctrl - until the page fits) and http://www.cjlab-attacker.com (a single button that leads to a *You have been hacked* page).
5. Look at the files you will edit during the lab: `defender/index.html`, `attacker/attacker.html`, `attacker/attacker.css`, `image_defender/apache_defender.conf`.
6. Get your flag: `sudo cjlab-verify 0`

> The files in `defender/` and `attacker/` are mounted into the containers: after editing them just reload the page (clear the browser cache with Ctrl+Shift+R if you do not see the change). Changes of the Apache configuration need a rebuild (Task 5).
levels.solution:
```
seed@seed:~$ cd ~/Labsetup
seed@seed:~/Labsetup$ dcbuild
seed@seed:~/Labsetup$ dcup            # stays in the foreground: use a 2nd terminal tab afterwards
seed@seed:~$ dockps
... defender-10.9.0.5
... attacker-10.9.0.105
seed@seed:~$ sudo cjlab-verify 0
```
Your flag is: `${ANSWER}`

hints.title: Which commands start the containers?
hints.content: From ~/Labsetup run `dcbuild` (= `docker-compose build`) and then `dcup` (= `docker-compose up`). `dcup` keeps running in the foreground: open a second terminal tab for the other commands, or use `docker-compose up -d`.

hints.title: The build fails or the sites do not answer
hints.content: Run `dockps` to see which container is missing. If the build cannot download the base image, retry `docker pull handsonsecurity/seed-server:apache`. If permission denied appears for docker, log out and in again. Then run `sudo cjlab-verify 0` and read the [FAIL] lines.

levels.title: Task 1 - Copy that site! (iframe)
levels.content:
# Task 1 - Copy that site!

The first step of the attacker is to make the malicious site look exactly like Alice's website. The usual trick is an HTML inline frame (`<iframe>`) that embeds another page: the `src` attribute tells which page is loaded inside.

## To do
* In ~/Labsetup/attacker/attacker.html add an `<iframe>` that loads http://www.cjlab.com (replace the TODO comment; the malicious `<button>` must stay after the iframe).
* In ~/Labsetup/attacker/attacker.css use height, width and position so that the iframe covers the whole page and the button is displayed over the iframe. Explicitly remove the border.
* Hints from the lab: look at the difference between `position: absolute` and `position: relative`.
* Reload http://www.cjlab-attacker.com and observe the result.
* Get your flag: `sudo cjlab-verify 1`

## For your lab report
**Q1.** With the iframe inserted, what does the attacker's website look like? (screenshot)

hints.title: iframe syntax
hints.content: An iframe is written `<iframe src="URL"></iframe>`. Put it in the `<body>`, before the `<button>` (elements that come later are drawn on top).

hints.title: Which CSS properties?
hints.content: Give the iframe `width: 100%; height: 100%; border: none;`. To let it fill the page from the top-left corner use `position: absolute; top: 0; left: 0;` (an absolutely positioned element is removed from the normal flow, just like the given button).

hints.title: Why does my page look different from Alice's?
hints.content: Browsers add default margins/borders. Check that border is none and that there is no scroll bar: 100% width and height. Clear the cache (`Ctrl+Shift+R`). Then run `sudo cjlab-verify 1` and read the [FAIL] lines.

levels.title: Task 2 - Let's get clickjacking! (invisible button)
levels.content:
# Task 2 - Let's get clickjacking!

Now hide the malicious button exactly over Alice's *Explore Menu* button, so that a visitor who thinks they click *Explore Menu* actually clicks your button.

## To do
Edit the button rule of ~/Labsetup/attacker/attacker.css (the parts marked `TODO`):
* make the button invisible but still clickable;
* move it so that it covers the *Explore Menu* button of the framed page (e.g. `margin-left` and `margin-top`; adjust until it fits on your screen / zoom level).
* Test: click where *Explore Menu* is displayed on http://www.cjlab-attacker.com - you must land on the *You have been hacked* page.
* Get your flag: `sudo cjlab-verify 2`

## For your lab report
**Q2.** How does the appearance of the attacker's site compare to the defender's site?
**Q3.** What happens when you click on *Explore Menu* on the attacker's site?
**Q4.** Describe an attack scenario in which this style of clickjacking leads to undesirable consequences for a victim user.

hints.title: How to make an element invisible but clickable?
hints.content: An element with `display: none` or `visibility: hidden` cannot be clicked at all. Instead make it transparent: `opacity: 0;` or set both `color` and `background-color` to `transparent`.

hints.title: How do I find the position of Explore Menu?
hints.content: Open http://www.cjlab.com, press F12, click the element picker and hover over *Explore Menu*: the developer tools show its size and position. Remember the attacker's button is `position: absolute`, so `margin-left` / `margin-top` (or `left` / `top`) move it relative to the top-left corner of the page. Make the attacker's button temporarily visible (e.g. blue background) while you tune the values.

hints.title: Starting values
hints.content: On a standard layout *Explore Menu* is about 45-50 px from the left and 340-350 px from the top. Try `margin-left: 45px; margin-top: 345px;` and adjust. Keep the button's onclick pointing to hacked.html.

levels.title: Task 3 - Bust that frame! (frame-busting script)
levels.content:
# Task 3 - Bust that frame!

Time to switch sides. Frame busting prevents a page from being displayed inside a frame of another site. You will add a JavaScript frame-buster to Alice's page.

## To do
Open ~/Labsetup/defender/index.html and fill in the (empty) JavaScript function `makeThisFrameOnTop()`:
* compare `window.top` and `window.self` to find out whether the top window and the current window are the same object (they should be);
* if they differ, use the Location object to set the location of the top window to the location of the current window.

It takes only a few lines. Reload http://www.cjlab-attacker.com to see whether the attacker is stopped, then get your flag: `sudo cjlab-verify 3`

## For your lab report
**Q5.** What happens when you navigate to the attacker's site now?
**Q6.** What happens when you click the button?

hints.title: What do window.top and window.self mean?
hints.content: `window.self` is the window the script runs in; `window.top` is the topmost window of the tab. In a normal page both are the same object. Inside an iframe `window.top` is the parent page.

hints.title: How to change the location?
hints.content: `window.location` is a Location object: assigning to it navigates the window. So you can assign to `window.top.location`.

hints.title: Skeleton

levels.title: Task 4 - Bust the buster! (sandbox attribute)
levels.content:
# Task 4 - Bust the buster!

Back to the attacker. Front-end defenses such as frame busting run in the victim's browser, inside the page the attacker controls the frame of, so the attacker can neutralise them. One of the simplest workarounds here is the `sandbox` attribute of the `<iframe>`.

## To do
* Read about the sandbox attribute of iframes (MDN: *iframe - sandbox*).
* Add the sandbox attribute to the iframe in ~/Labsetup/attacker/attacker.html so that the frame-buster of the defender can no longer redirect the top window. Do not remove the frame-busting script of Task 3 and keep your Task 1-2 attack intact.
* Reload http://www.cjlab-attacker.com and click on the (invisible) button.
* Get your flag: `sudo cjlab-verify 4`

## For your lab report
**Q7.** What does the `sandbox` attribute do? Why does it prevent the frame buster from working?
**Q8.** What happens when you navigate to the attacker's site after the change?
**Q9.** What happens when you click the button on the attacker's site?
levels.solution:
`attacker.html`
```html
<iframe src="http://www.cjlab.com" sandbox></iframe>
```
With an empty sandbox attribute the framed page is treated as a unique origin, scripts are blocked and it cannot navigate the top-level window (no `allow-scripts`, no `allow-top-navigation`) - so `makeThisFrameOnTop()` never runs / can never replace the attacker's page. Then `sudo cjlab-verify 4`. Your flag is: `${ANSWER}`

hints.title: Where do I put the attribute?
hints.content: Directly in the opening tag of the iframe, next to src: `<iframe src="..." sandbox></iframe>`.

hints.title: What does sandbox do?
hints.content: `sandbox` applies extra restrictions to the framed content. Each restriction is lifted only if you list the matching token (`allow-scripts`, `allow-forms`, `allow-top-navigation`, ...). Think about which restriction stops the defender's JavaScript.

hints.title: My flag is refused
hints.content: The checker requires the sandbox attribute without allow-top-navigation and without allow-scripts, and your Tasks 1-3 must still be in place. Run `sudo cjlab-verify 4` and read the [FAIL] lines.

levels.title: Task 5 - The ultimate bust (HTTP response headers)
levels.content:
# Task 5 - The ultimate bust

Front-end defenses can be circumvented, so the server must tell the browser not to display the page in a frame. Two HTTP response headers do that:

* `X-Frame-Options` (XFO) - the older one;
* `Content-Security-Policy` (CSP) - the newer, more powerful one. The directive relevant to clickjacking is `frame-ancestors`.

## To do
1. Open ~/Labsetup/image_defender/apache_defender.conf. The header lines are commented out: uncomment them and fill them in:
   * X-Frame-Options = `DENY`
   * `Content-Security-Policy` containing the directive `frame-ancestors 'none'`
2. The configuration is copied into the image, so rebuild and restart: `dcdown`, `dcbuild`, `dcup`.
3. Check the headers: `curl -I http://www.cjlab.com`
4. Test the attacker's site after each header, one at a time, then with both.
5. Get your flag: `sudo cjlab-verify 5`

## For your lab report
**Q10.** What is the `X-Frame-Options` header and why is it set to DENY to prevent the attack?
**Q11.** What is the `Content-Security-Policy` header and why is it set to `frame-ancestors 'none'` to prevent the attack?
**Q12.** What happens when you navigate to the attacker's site after modifying each response header (one at a time)? What do you see when you click the button?
levels.solution:
`image_defender/apache_defender.conf`
```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    DocumentRoot /var/www/defender
    ServerName www.cjlab.com
    Header set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
    Header set Content-Security-Policy " \
             frame-ancestors 'none'; \
           "
</VirtualHost>
```
```
seed@seed:~/Labsetup$ dcdown && dcbuild && dcup
seed@seed:~$ curl -I http://www.cjlab.com      # X-Frame-Options and Content-Security-Policy are present
seed@seed:~$ sudo cjlab-verify 5
```
Your flag is: `${ANSWER}`

hints.title: Syntax of a header in Apache
hints.content: In an Apache VirtualHost, `Header set <Header-name> "<value>"` adds a response header. The two header names are `X-Frame-Options` and `Content-Security-Policy`.

hints.title: My change has no effect / Apache refuses to start
hints.content: The conf file is baked into the Docker image: you must `dcdown`, `dcbuild`, `dcup`. Also: the placeholder line in the file ends with a `;` - a Header directive must not end with `;` (only the CSP *value* uses `;` after a directive). Check the logs of `dcup` for syntax errors.

hints.title: Full lines
hints.content:
```apache
Header set X-Frame-Options "DENY"
Header set Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'none';"
```
(Keep them inside `<VirtualHost> ... </VirtualHost>`.) Verify with `curl -I http://www.cjlab.com`.

levels.title: Final quiz - what did you observe?

choices.text: Tricking a user into clicking something different from what they perceive, typically by overlaying a hidden element on a legitimate page
Stealing the session cookie by injecting JavaScript into a web page
Intercepting the traffic between a browser and a web server
Guessing the password of a user with a dictionary attack

questions.text: Which HTML element did the attacker use to load Alice's website inside the malicious page?

choices.text: <embed-site>
<link>
<frameset-redirect>
<iframe>

questions.text: Which CSS declaration makes the malicious button invisible while it can still receive the victim's click?

choices.text: visibility: hidden;
z-index: -1;
opacity: 0;
display: none;

questions.text: What does the frame-busting script compare?

choices.text: window.opener and window.name
window.top and window.self
window.parent and document.referrer
window.location and document.domain

questions.text: Why does the sandbox attribute defeat the JavaScript frame-buster?

choices.text: Sandboxed frames cannot run scripts or navigate the top-level window unless the matching allow-* tokens are given
It encrypts the content of the framed page
It makes the browser ignore the src attribute
It hides the framed page from the victim

questions.text: Why are front-end defenses such as frame busting NOT sufficient against clickjacking?

choices.text: They slow down the server too much
They only work with HTTPS
Browsers refuse to run JavaScript inside iframes
They run in the victim's browser, in a context the attacker controls, so the attacker can neutralise them

questions.text: What does the header 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' tell the browser?

choices.text: Display this page in frames of a list of trusted sites
Block all JavaScript of this page
Never display this page in a frame, whichever site tries to embed it (even the same origin)
Display this page in frames of the same origin only

questions.text: Which Content-Security-Policy directive specifies the valid parents that may embed a page in a frame? (answer with the directive name only)

choices.text: frame-ancestors

levels.instructions: 8 questions, 5 points each (= 0.5 / 20 each). Answer from what you did and observed in the lab.

levels.title: Debriefing and lab report
levels.content:
# Well done!

You attacked a website with clickjacking and then defended it in three stages. Remember the lessons:

* Front-end (JavaScript) defenses are bypassable - the attacker controls the frame in which your code runs.
* Back-end defenses are robust: send `X-Frame-Options` and/or `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` so that the *browser* refuses to render your page inside a hostile frame. Prefer `frame-ancestors` (it is more flexible: it can also allow specific trusted parents, e.g. `frame-ancestors 'self' https://partner.example`); keeping both gives coverage for older browsers.
* Defense in depth: also protect sensitive actions with re-authentication / anti-CSRF tokens and `SameSite` cookies.

## Lab report (to hand in to your teacher)
Describe what you did and observed, with screenshots, and give an explanation of the important code snippets (code without explanation earns no credit). Answer the questions Q1 to Q12 that were listed in the levels. Further reading: OWASP *Clickjacking* page.

You can now close your sandbox session; the sandbox will be deleted by your instructor.
